content:
A hands-on electrical-engineering course built around an Arduino Uno and a
breadboard. Every unit pairs real theory (Ohm, Kirchhoff, RC circuits, diodes,
transistors, ADCs, timers, motors, serial protocols, power) with a lab where you
PREDICT a value, BUILD the circuit, MEASURE it with your multimeter and compare.
You'll build an LED curve tracer, a capacitance meter, a 555 + Arduino frequency
counter, a sonar theremin, a sun-tracking servo, an optical serial link you
decode yourself, and finally your own 4-mode bench meter and a homemade
oscilloscope. Written for people who already know how to blink an LED.

### How every unit works

1. **Theory** — read it, then take the theory test.
2. **Labs** — predict a value, build the circuit, measure it with your multimeter, then type your predictions and real readings into the lab test.
3. Your readings are graded against the expected value with a tolerance, because real parts are never exact.

content.text:
**Board:** Arduino Uno R3 (or a Nano / Uno clone with an ATmega328P). Uno R4 notes are in the lessons where they matter.

**Tools**

- Digital multimeter (DC volts, DC mA, ohms, diode test; capacitance mode is a bonus)
- USB cable, computer with Arduino IDE 2
- Ruler or tape measure (Unit 8)

content.text:
**Safety**

- Nothing in this module touches mains (230 V). Never connect anything here to a wall socket.
- Arduino pins take 0–5 V only. Never put a negative voltage or more than 5 V on any pin — use a divider.
- A single pin: 20 mA recommended, 40 mA absolute maximum. The whole chip: 200 mA.
- Electrolytic capacitors have polarity: stripe = minus. Reversed, they can bulge or pop.
- Motors and servos get their own supply when possible. Always connect the grounds together.
- Measure current with the meter in SERIES and the red lead in the mA socket. Move it back to V afterwards — a meter left on mA shorts whatever you probe next.
- If something gets hot or smells, unplug USB first, think second.

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Calibrate your tools — and your instincts

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Know exactly which breadboard holes are connected (and which rails are split)
- Use all four multimeter modes correctly: V, mA, Ω, diode/continuity
- Read resistor colour codes and capacitor number codes without a chart
- Know the Arduino Uno's electrical limits before you push them

content:
You already know how to blink an LED, so this unit is a fast calibration pass. Every later lab asks you to **predict → build → measure → compare**, and that only works if you trust your tools.

### The breadboard
Each short row of 5 holes is one node. The groove in the middle separates the two halves. The long rails along the edges are power buses — but on many 830-point boards **each rail is split in the middle**. A circuit that "works on the left half only" is almost always a split rail. Check yours with continuity mode once and you'll never lose an hour to it again.

### The multimeter

| Mode | How it connects | What it does to the circuit |
|---|---|---|
| **DC V** | in **parallel** (across the part) | almost nothing — input resistance ≈ 10 MΩ |
| **DC mA** | in **series** (break the circuit, meter becomes a wire) | adds a small *burden voltage* |
| **Ω** | across the part, **power OFF** | injects its own tiny current |
| **Diode / continuity** | across the part, power off | shows forward voltage / beeps below ~30–50 Ω |

The most common way to blow a meter fuse: measuring voltage while the red lead is still in the mA socket. In that socket the meter is nearly a short circuit.

### Colour codes
4-band resistors: **digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance**. Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. Gold tolerance = ±5 %, brown = ±1 %. 5-band resistors have three digits before the multiplier.
Example: yellow-violet-red-gold = 4, 7, ×100 = **4.7 kΩ ±5 %**.

Resistor values come from the **E-series**: E12 is 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82 (× powers of ten). That's why you'll never find a 25 kΩ resistor in a kit.

Ceramic capacitors print **two digits + number of zeros, in picofarads**: 104 = 10 × 10⁴ pF = 100 000 pF = **100 nF**. 103 = 10 nF, 473 = 47 nF.

### The Uno's limits (ATmega328P at 5 V)
- Any pin: **0 to 5 V only**.
- Current per pin: 20 mA recommended, **40 mA absolute maximum**.
- Whole chip (all pins together): **200 mA**.
- 5 V pin on USB power: shared with the board, protected by a 500 mA polyfuse.
- 3.3 V pin: small regulator, budget it at ~50 mA on a classic Uno.

These numbers will come back in every unit. Units 4 and 6 are basically about working *around* them.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Resistor code | R = (d1 d2) × 10^multiplier |
| Capacitor code | C [pF] = (d1 d2) × 10^d3   (104 → 100 nF) |

**Remember**

- **Voltmeter connects…** — In PARALLEL (across the part). ~10 MΩ input, barely disturbs the circuit.
- **Ammeter connects…** — In SERIES (break the circuit). The meter becomes part of the wire.
- **104 on a capacitor** — 10 × 10⁴ pF = 100 nF
- **E12 series** — 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82 (× powers of 10)
- **ATmega328P pin current limits** — 20 mA recommended, 40 mA absolute max, 200 mA whole chip
- **Gold / silver / brown tolerance band** — ±5 % / ±10 % / ±1 %
- **Colour digits 0–9** — Black, Brown, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Grey, White

lessons.title: Lab: Know your bench
lessons.summary: Verify your breadboard, meter and parts before trusting them in later labs.
content:
**Goal:** Verify your breadboard, meter and parts before trusting them in later labs.

About 30 minutes.

content.text:
**You need**

- Breadboard, a few jumpers
- Three resistors from the kit (any values)
- A 104 ceramic capacitor
- A red LED
- Arduino Uno + USB

content:
### Step by step

1. Set the meter to continuity. Probe the two ends of each long power rail. Mark on the board (tape or marker) if a rail is split in the middle.
2. Probe two holes in the same 5-hole row (beep) and two holes across the centre groove (no beep).
3. **Read** → lab test, question 1: Before measuring: find a resistor with the bands brown, black, orange, gold. What is its value?
4. **Measure** → lab test, question 2: Measure that 10 kΩ resistor in Ω mode (don't touch both leads with your fingers — your body is in parallel!).
5. **Write down:** Read and then measure your other two resistors. Record the bigger one in Ω. (Ω)
6. Put the meter in diode-test mode. Red probe on the LED's long leg (anode), black on the short leg. The LED should glow faintly.
7. **Write down:** Diode-test reading for the red LED (the meter shows the forward voltage in V or mV). (V)
8. Plug in the Arduino by USB. Meter on DC V. Black probe on a GND header pin.
9. **Measure** → lab test, question 3: Measure the 5V header pin. (USB 5 V passes through a fuse and a protection MOSFET on the Uno, so expect a bit under 5.00.)
10. **Measure** → lab test, question 4: Measure the 3.3V header pin.

content.text: Do the steps on your breadboard first. Then open the **lab test** below and type in your predictions and the real readings from your multimeter or Serial Monitor.

**What you should see**

You now have three personal reference numbers: your real 5 V rail, your meter's LED forward voltage, and whether your rails are split. Keep them — later labs use them.

content:
### If it doesn't work

- **Resistor reads way too low** — You're touching both leads with your fingers, or it's still in a circuit. Measure it loose.
- **LED doesn't light in diode mode** — Swap the probes (wrong polarity), or your meter's test voltage is too low for blue/white LEDs — that's normal.
- **5V pin reads ~4.3 V** — A weak USB port/hub or a long thin cable. Try another port; remember the number for Unit 1.

content.text:
**Challenges**

- Find the burden voltage of your meter: put it in series with a 1 kΩ resistor and LED on 5 V, measure the current on the mA range and on the µA range (if it has one), and compare.

Before measuring: find a resistor with the bands brown, black, orange, gold. What is its value?

Answer in ohms, e.g. 4700 for 4.7 kΩ.

**Measure:** Measure that 10 kΩ resistor in Ω mode (don't touch both leads with your fingers — your body is in parallel!).

Type the value you actually read.
tasks.explain: Anything from 9.5 kΩ to 10.5 kΩ is inside a ±5 % part's tolerance. Most real parts are much closer.

**Measure:** Measure the 5V header pin. (USB 5 V passes through a fuse and a protection MOSFET on the Uno, so expect a bit under 5.00.)

Type the value you actually read.
tasks.explain: Typical readings are 4.7–5.1 V on USB. Write your exact value down — Unit 1 shows why this number matters for every analogRead().

tasks.prompt:
**Measure:** Measure the 3.3V header pin.

Type the value you actually read.
tasks.explain: That comes from a small dedicated regulator, so it's usually very close to 3.30 V.

units.title: Divider Detective
units.description: Ohm, Kirchhoff, and why your voltmeter lies to you a little

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Ohm, Kirchhoff, and why your voltmeter lies to you a little

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Apply Ohm's law, power and both Kirchhoff laws to real circuits
- Replace any divider with its Thevenin equivalent and predict loading
- Understand what the ADC's reference voltage does to every reading
- Measure your Arduino's real 5 V rail with its internal bandgap reference

content:
### Three laws you'll use every day
**Ohm:** V = I · R. **Power:** P = V · I = I² · R = V² / R.
**KCL (current law):** the currents into a node add up to the currents out of it — charge doesn't pile up in a wire.
**KVL (voltage law):** going around any closed loop, the voltage rises and drops add up to zero.

### The voltage divider
Two resistors in series between Vin and ground. The same current flows through both (KCL), so each one takes a share of the voltage proportional to its resistance (KVL + Ohm):

**Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2)**

It's the most used circuit in electronics: sensors (Unit 7), level shifting, measuring voltages above 5 V (Capstone 1), biasing.

### The catch: loading
That formula assumes **nothing** is connected to Vout. Connect a load R_L and it sits in parallel with R2:

**Vout = Vin · (R2 ∥ R_L) / (R1 + R2 ∥ R_L)**, where R2 ∥ R_L = R2·R_L / (R2 + R_L)

The clean way to think about it is **Thevenin's theorem**: any linear circuit seen from two terminals behaves like *one voltage source in series with one resistor*. For a divider:

- V_th = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2) (the unloaded output)
- R_th = R1 ∥ R2 (turn Vin into a wire and look back in)

A 10 k/10 k divider has R_th = 5 kΩ. A 1 M/1 M divider has R_th = 500 kΩ — a hundred times "weaker". Your multimeter's 10 MΩ input is a load too: on the 1 M/1 M divider it pulls the reading from 2.50 V down to about 2.38 V. You'll measure this.

### What the ADC actually measures
analogRead() returns **ADC = Vin × 1024 / Vref**, from 0 to 1023. On the Uno, Vref defaults to the **5 V rail itself** (AVcc). So a reading is only as good as your 5 V rail. If USB gives you 4.80 V and your code assumes 5.00, every voltage is 4 % too high.

Fix: the ATmega328P has an internal **1.1 V bandgap reference**. Measure *it* with AVcc as reference: ADC = 1.1 × 1024 / Vcc, so **Vcc = 1.1 × 1024 / ADC**. The bandgap varies chip to chip (about 1.0–1.2 V), so you calibrate it once against your multimeter and then your Arduino knows its own supply.

### Why the ADC wants R_th ≤ 10 kΩ
Inside the ADC is a tiny *sample-and-hold* capacitor (~14 pF). When analogRead() starts, it connects that cap to the pin for a short window. If your source is weak (high R_th), the cap doesn't fully charge — especially right after it held a different channel's voltage. The datasheet recommends ≤ 10 kΩ source impedance. The 1 M/1 M divider breaks that rule on purpose so you can see what happens. The usual fixes: lower resistor values, a dummy read after switching channels, or a 100 nF capacitor from the pin to ground (a local charge reservoir).

> **Uno R4 note:** the R4 ADC is different (12–14 bit, `analogReadResolution()`), and the bandgap trick in this lab's sketch is ATmega-only. Everything else applies.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Ohm's law | V = I · R |
| Power | P = V · I = I²R = V²/R |
| Divider | Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2) |
| Parallel | R1 ∥ R2 = R1·R2 / (R1 + R2) |
| Thevenin of a divider | Vth = Vin·R2/(R1+R2),  Rth = R1 ∥ R2 |
| ADC (Uno) | ADC = Vin · 1024 / Vref |
| Supply from bandgap | Vcc = Vbg · 1024 / ADC(bandgap) |

**Remember**

- **KCL** — Sum of currents into a node = sum of currents out.
- **KVL** — Sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop = 0.
- **Divider formula** — Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2)
- **Thevenin resistance of a divider** — R1 ∥ R2 (source replaced by a wire)
- **ADC formula on Uno** — ADC = Vin × 1024 / Vref, range 0–1023
- **Measuring Vcc with the bandgap** — Vcc = 1.1 V × 1024 / ADC(bandgap). Calibrate the 1.1 V per chip.
- **ADC source impedance limit** — ≤ 10 kΩ recommended (sample-and-hold cap must settle)
- **Typical DMM input resistance** — 10 MΩ — still a load on megaohm circuits

What is the Thevenin resistance of that 22 k/10 k divider, in kΩ?
A 100 Ω resistor sits directly across 5 V. How much power does it dissipate, in watts?
tasks.explain: V²/R = 25/100 = 0.25 W — exactly the rating of a typical ¼ W resistor. It will get hot; real designs keep ≥ 2× margin.

tasks.prompt: Three wires meet at a node. 4 mA flows in on wire A, 1 mA flows in on wire B. What flows on wire C?
tasks.explain: KCL: everything in must come out. 4 + 1 = 5 mA must leave on C.

tasks.prompt: Using smaller resistors (e.g. 1 k/1 k instead of 100 k/100 k) makes a divider less sensitive to loading but wastes more power.
tasks.explain: Lower R_th = stiffer output, but the divider current I = Vin/(R1+R2) goes up. Every divider is that trade-off.

tasks.prompt: analogRead returns 512 while the real 5V rail is 4.80 V. What is the real input voltage? (ADC = Vin·1024/Vref)
tasks.explain: 512 × 4.80 / 1024 = 2.40 V. Code that assumes 5.00 V would report 2.50 V — 4 % wrong.

tasks.prompt: The bandgap channel reads ADC = 230 and your chip's bandgap is 1.10 V. What is Vcc?
Why does the ATmega's ADC prefer sources of 10 kΩ or less?
options: Its sample-and-hold capacitor must charge fully during a short sampling window
The ADC only works with currents above 1 mA
10 kΩ is the internal pull-up value
tasks.explain: The ~14 pF sample cap charges through the source resistance. Too high R_th → it doesn't settle in time.
raw * 5 / 1024 is computed entirely in integers (the fraction is thrown away) BEFORE being stored in a float. Write raw * 5.0 / 1024.0.

tasks.prompt: Put the Thevenin method for a loaded divider in order.
items: Find V_th = unloaded output voltage
Short the source and find R_th looking back into the output
Draw V_th in series with R_th
Attach the load and solve the simple series circuit
tasks.explain: Once you have V_th and R_th, any load is just one more series divider.

lessons.title: Lab: Divider Detective
lessons.summary: Predict, build and measure a stiff and a weak divider — with the meter and with the Arduino — and catch loading in the act.
content:
**Goal:** Predict, build and measure a stiff and a weak divider — with the meter and with the Arduino — and catch loading in the act.

About 60 minutes.

content.text:
**You need**

- 2 × 10 kΩ, 2 × 1 MΩ resistors
- Jumpers, multimeter
- Arduino Uno

content.caption: Schematic

content:
### Wiring

| From | To |
|---|---|
| Arduino 5V | top of R1 and top of R3 |
| R1/R2 junction | A0 |
| R3/R4 junction | A1 |
| bottom of R2 and R4 | Arduino GND |

content.title: u01_voltmeter.ino
content.caption: Copy it into Arduino IDE 2 (board: Arduino Uno). Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.

content:
### Step by step

1. **Predict** → lab test, question 1: Predict: Vout of the 10 k/10 k divider fed with exactly 5.00 V.
2. **Predict** → lab test, question 2: Predict: the current flowing through the 10 k/10 k divider, in mA.
3. Build both dividers on the breadboard from the schematic. Don't connect A0/A1 yet.
4. **Measure** → lab test, question 3: Meter on DC V: measure the 10 k/10 k midpoint (A0 node) to GND.
5. **Predict** → lab test, question 4: Predict what a 10 MΩ multimeter will read on the 1 M/1 M midpoint (5.00 V supply). Hint: R4 ∥ 10 MΩ.
6. **Measure** → lab test, question 5: Now measure the 1 M/1 M midpoint (A1 node) with your meter.
7. Connect the R1/R2 midpoint to A0 and the R3/R4 midpoint to A1. Upload u01_voltmeter and open the Serial Monitor at 115200.
8. Measure your 5V pin with the meter. Type numbers like 1080, 1100, 1120 into the Serial Monitor until the sketch's Vcc matches your meter (that's your chip's bandgap in mV).
9. **Write down:** Your calibrated bandgap value (you'll reuse it in Capstone 1). (mV)
10. **Write down:** A0 'V(real Vcc)' reading from the sketch. (V)
11. **Write down:** A1 'V(real Vcc)' reading from the sketch. (V)
12. Edit the sketch: delete the line `analogRead(pin); // dummy read` in readAveraged(), upload again, and watch A1.
13. **Check** → lab test, question 6: What happened to the A1 reading without the dummy read?

content.text: Do the steps on your breadboard first. Then open the **lab test** below and type in your predictions and the real readings from your multimeter or Serial Monitor.

**What you should see**

The stiff divider reads the same everywhere. The weak one reads differently depending on WHAT you measure it with — the meter, the ADC, or the ADC right after another channel. That's loading and source impedance, and it's why sensor dividers in this course use 10 kΩ.

content:
### If it doesn't work

- **A0 reads 1023** — The midpoint is connected to 5 V — check that A0 goes to the junction, not the top.
- **Vcc shows something crazy like 20 V** — You typed a value outside 900–1300; the sketch ignores those. Reset and type again.
- **Readings jump around by several counts** — Normal ADC noise is ±1–2 counts. More than that: loose jumper or long wires near the motor/USB cable.

content.text:
**Challenges**

- Add a 100 nF capacitor from A1 to GND (keep the dummy read deleted). Does the 1 M/1 M reading become stable again? Explain why with the sample-and-hold cap.
- Switch the ADC reference to the internal 1.1 V with analogReference(INTERNAL) and measure a divider that outputs < 1 V (e.g. 100 kΩ over 10 kΩ). Compare the resolution.

tasks.prompt: Predict: Vout of the 10 k/10 k divider fed with exactly 5.00 V.
tasks.explain: Equal resistors split the voltage in half.

tasks.prompt: Predict: the current flowing through the 10 k/10 k divider, in mA.
tasks.explain: 5 V / 20 kΩ = 0.25 mA. A divider always wastes some current — here 1.25 mW.

tasks.prompt:
**Measure:** Meter on DC V: measure the 10 k/10 k midpoint (A0 node) to GND.

Type the value you actually read.
tasks.explain: If your 5 V rail is 4.9 V, expect 2.45 V. The divider scales whatever the supply really is.

tasks.prompt: Predict what a 10 MΩ multimeter will read on the 1 M/1 M midpoint (5.00 V supply). Hint: R4 ∥ 10 MΩ.
tasks.explain: 1 MΩ ∥ 10 MΩ = 0.909 MΩ, so Vout = 5 × 0.909 / 1.909 = 2.38 V. The meter changed the thing it measured.

tasks.prompt:
**Measure:** Now measure the 1 M/1 M midpoint (A1 node) with your meter.

Type the value you actually read.
tasks.explain: Close to 2.38 V instead of 2.50 V = loading. (Some cheap meters have 1 MΩ input: then you'd see 1.67 V!)

tasks.prompt: What happened to the A1 reading without the dummy read?
options: It moved (usually towards the A0 value / became less stable)
tasks.explain: With 500 kΩ source impedance, the ADC's sample cap still 'remembers' the previous channel (A0). The dummy read gives it time to settle. On the stiff A0 divider you won't see any difference.

units.title: Trace the Curve
units.description: Diodes and LEDs are not resistors — prove it with your own I-V tracer

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Diodes and LEDs are not resistors — prove it with your own I-V tracer

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Explain the exponential I-V curve of a PN junction
- Measure forward voltage vs colour and relate it to the semiconductor's band gap
- Size an LED resistor from the curve instead of guessing
- Use a diode as a thermometer

content:
### A resistor is a straight line. A diode is a cliff.
Plot current against voltage for a resistor and you get a straight line through zero with slope 1/R. For a diode you get almost nothing until a "knee", then current shoots up. The ideal-diode (Shockley) equation:

**I = Iₛ · (e^(V / (n·V_T)) − 1)**

- Iₛ is a tiny saturation current (pA–nA range).
- V_T = kT/q ≈ **26 mV** at room temperature (the *thermal voltage*).
- n is the ideality factor, 1–2 for silicon, often 1.5–3 for LEDs.

Because it's exponential, every extra **n × 60 mV** multiplies the current by **10**. That is why you never drive an LED from a "voltage": a tiny voltage change is a huge current change, and the LED's Vf also drops as it warms up — runaway. You set the **current** with a series resistor instead:

**R = (V_supply − V_f) / I_LED**

### Why colours have different forward voltages
A photon's energy is set by the semiconductor's band gap, and the electron needs at least roughly that much energy (in eV) to cross it. Red light (~630 nm) photons carry ~2.0 eV, blue (~465 nm) ~2.7 eV. So, roughly: **red ≈ 1.8–2.1 V, yellow/green ≈ 2.0–2.2 V (older) or 2.8–3.2 V (pure green InGaN), blue/white ≈ 2.8–3.3 V.** You're about to measure the real numbers for your kit.

### Diode facts worth knowing
- Silicon rectifier (1N4007): knee around 0.5–0.7 V at small currents, ~0.9–1 V at 1 A. Rated 1 A, 1000 V reverse.
- LEDs survive only ~5 V in reverse. Don't plug them backwards into anything above that.
- Forward voltage has a **temperature coefficient of about −2 mV/°C** for silicon. Warm the diode, Vf drops. Many chip thermometers are literally this.
- Don't share one resistor between parallel LEDs: the one with the slightly lower Vf hogs the current (exponential curve again!).

### How the tracer works
You can't measure current directly with the ADC, but you can measure voltage at two points. A known **sense resistor** in series turns current into a voltage: I = (V_A0 − V_A1) / R_sense. The pot acts as an adjustable voltage source. Sweep it, log both voltages, and you have an I-V curve.

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Use Q = CV and I = C·dV/dt to reason about capacitors
- Predict an RC charging curve and the 63 % / 5τ rules
- Measure capacitance by timing an RC charge
- Turn PWM into a real analog voltage with an RC low-pass filter and trade ripple vs speed

content:
### What a capacitor does
A capacitor stores charge: **Q = C · V**. Differentiate and you get the rule that explains everything else:

**I = C · dV/dt**

A capacitor's voltage *cannot jump*. Pushing current into it changes its voltage at a rate set by C. Energy stored: **E = ½ C V²**.

### Charging through a resistor
Connect a discharged C to a voltage V_s through R. At first the cap is at 0 V so the full V_s is across R and the current is V_s/R. As the cap charges, less voltage is left across R, so the current — and the charging rate — falls. The result is an exponential:

**V(t) = V_s · (1 − e^(−t/τ))**, with **τ = R · C**

| time | 1τ | 2τ | 3τ | 4.6τ | 5τ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| charge | 63.2 % | 86.5 % | 95.0 % | 99 % | 99.3 % |

Discharging is the mirror image: V(t) = V₀ · e^(−t/τ). "Five tau" is the engineering meaning of "fully charged".

**Your capacitance meter is just this equation run backwards:** charge through a known R, time how long it takes to hit 63.2 % (that's τ), and C = τ / R. With τ in µs and R in Ω, C comes out in µF directly.

### Real capacitors
- **Ceramic** (e.g. 104 = 100 nF): small, no polarity, great at high frequency. Cheap ones (Y5V) can be −20 %/+80 % off and drift with voltage.
- **Electrolytic** (10 µF, 100 µF…): large values, **polarised** (stripe = −), typically ±20 % tolerance. Your meter will find that out.

### The RC low-pass filter and the PWM DAC
The same R and C, used as a filter, pass slow changes and block fast ones. The **cut-off frequency** is **f_c = 1 / (2π R C)**.

analogWrite() doesn't make an analog voltage — it switches a pin between 0 and 5 V about 490 times a second (pins 5 and 6: ~980 Hz). The *average* is D · 5 V, where D is the duty cycle. An RC filter with f_c far below 490 Hz extracts that average. What's left over is **ripple**. For small ripple:

**ΔV_pp ≈ V · D · (1 − D) / (f_PWM · R · C)**

Bigger RC → less ripple but a slower response (≈ 5τ to settle after a change). That's the fundamental speed vs. smoothness trade-off of every filter, and you'll see both sides of it on the Serial Plotter.

|---|---|
| Charge | Q = C · V |
| Capacitor current | I = C · dV/dt |
| Energy | E = ½ C V² |
| Time constant | τ = R · C |
| Charging | V(t) = Vs · (1 − e^(−t/τ)) |
| Low-pass cut-off | f_c = 1 / (2π R C) |
| PWM ripple (small-ripple approx.) | ΔVpp ≈ V·D·(1−D) / (f·R·C) |

**Remember**

- **Capacitor current** — I = C · dV/dt
- **Time constant** — τ = R·C (Ω × F = s)
- **Charge after 1τ / 5τ** — 63.2 % / 99.3 %
- **Measuring C with an Arduino** — Time to 63.2 % = τ → C = τ / R (µs / Ω = µF)
- **RC low-pass cut-off** — f_c = 1 / (2πRC)
- **Uno PWM frequencies** — ~490 Hz (pins 3, 9, 10, 11), ~980 Hz (pins 5, 6)
- **Electrolytic polarity** — Stripe = minus. Typical tolerance ±20 %.

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Explain cut-off, active and saturation regions of an NPN transistor
- Design a base resistor with a 'forced beta' so the transistor really saturates
- Calculate transistor power dissipation and know when it gets hot
- Protect switches from inductive kick with a flyback diode

content:
### Why you need a transistor
An Arduino pin is happy at 20 mA. A small motor wants 100–400 mA, an LED strip amps. A transistor lets the pin's small current **control** a big current that comes from a separate supply.

### The NPN BJT in three regions
Current into the base (I_B) controls current from collector to emitter (I_C).
- **Cut-off:** I_B = 0 → I_C ≈ 0. Switch OFF.
- **Active:** I_C = β · I_B. β (= h_FE) is roughly 100–300 and varies wildly between parts and with temperature. Great for amplifiers, terrible for switches, because V_CE can be several volts → the transistor dissipates **P = V_CE · I_C** and heats up.
- **Saturation:** you push more base current than the load needs. I_C is then limited by the *load*, not by β, and V_CE drops to **0.1–0.3 V**. Switch fully ON, barely warm.

Base–emitter behaves like a diode: **V_BE ≈ 0.65–0.8 V** when conducting.

### Designing the switch (low-side)
Put the load between +V and the collector, emitter to GND. Then:
1. Find the load current I_C (measure it!).
2. Choose a **forced beta** of 10–20 (not the datasheet β): I_B = I_C / 10.
3. **R_B = (V_pin − V_BE) / I_B.**

Example: a 4-LED bank drawing ~53 mA. I_B = 5.3 mA → R_B = (5 − 0.7)/5.3 mA ≈ 810 Ω → use 1 kΩ (4.3 mA, forced β ≈ 12). Saturated, and the pin is relaxed.

Why **low-side**? The emitter sits at GND, so a 5 V pin can always drive the base 0.7 V above it — even if the load runs on 12 V. A high-side NPN would need its base *above* the load voltage.

### Inductive kick
A motor is a coil. Coils resist changes in current: **V = L · dI/dt**. When the transistor snaps off, dI/dt is huge and the coil produces a voltage spike — easily tens of volts — that punches through the transistor. A **flyback diode** across the coil (cathode/stripe to +V) gives that current a safe loop to die out in. With PWM you switch hundreds of times a second, so the diode isn't optional.

### Beyond the BJT
- **Darlington pair:** two BJTs, β ≈ β₁·β₂ (≈ 10 000), but V_BE ≈ 1.4 V and V_CE(sat) ≈ 1 V. Your ULN2003 (Unit 10) is seven of these.
- **Logic-level MOSFET** (e.g. IRLZ44N): voltage-controlled, no steady gate current, R_DS(on) of tens of mΩ → amps with no heatsink. Needs a gate resistor (~100 Ω) and a pull-down (~100 kΩ). The modern default for big loads.

### Common ground
The load supply and the Arduino must share **GND**. Base current flows out of the pin, through B→E, and back to the Arduino through ground. No shared ground, no return path, no switching.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Active region | I_C = β · I_B |
| Base resistor | R_B = (V_pin − V_BE) / (I_C / β_forced),  β_forced ≈ 10–20 |
| Transistor dissipation | P = V_CE · I_C |
| Inductor voltage | V = L · dI/dt |
| Darlington gain | β ≈ β₁ · β₂ |

**Remember**

- **BJT saturation** — I_B more than enough → V_CE ≈ 0.1–0.3 V, I_C set by the load
- **Forced beta for switching** — 10–20, regardless of datasheet β
- **Base resistor** — R_B = (V_pin − 0.7) / I_B
- **Transistor heat** — P = V_CE × I_C — small when saturated
- **Flyback diode** — Across the coil, stripe to +V; absorbs the V = L·dI/dt spike
- **Darlington** — β ≈ β₁β₂, but V_BE ≈ 1.4 V and V_CE(sat) ≈ 1 V
- **Uno PWM pins** — 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11
- **Logic-level MOSFET** — Fully on at V_GS = 5 V (or less), tiny R_DS(on), gate resistor + pull-down

units.title: Clean Inputs
units.description: Floating pins, bouncing contacts and interrupts that don't lie

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Floating pins, bouncing contacts and interrupts that don't lie

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Explain why an unconnected CMOS input reads random values
- Know the ATmega's logic thresholds and what a Schmitt trigger is for
- See contact bounce, then remove it in hardware and in software
- Write correct interrupt code: short ISRs, volatile, atomic reads

content:
### A floating input is an antenna
A CMOS input has an input resistance in the hundreds of megaohms. If nothing drives it, a few picofarads of stray capacitance and the 50 Hz field from every mains cable in the room decide its state. It reads 0, 1, 0, 1… whatever it likes. Hence the **pull-up** (or pull-down) resistor: a weak, defined default that a button can easily overpower.

`pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP)` turns on a resistor inside the chip — **20–50 kΩ** on the ATmega328P. Pressed button to GND → LOW. Released → the pull-up pulls it HIGH.

### Logic thresholds
At Vcc = 5 V the ATmega328P guarantees:
- **LOW** if the input is below **0.3·Vcc = 1.5 V**
- **HIGH** if it is above **0.6·Vcc = 3.0 V**
- In between: undefined.

Digital inputs also have a **Schmitt trigger**: the threshold going up is higher than the threshold going down (hysteresis — you'll build the same idea in software in Unit 7). A slowly rising voltage therefore produces one clean edge instead of a burst.

### Contact bounce
A mechanical switch is two springy metal parts slamming together. They bounce for anywhere from tens of microseconds to several milliseconds, making and breaking contact many times. To a microcontroller that runs 16 million instructions a second, one press can look like 5 or 20 presses. Your bounce counter will show the real numbers for your buttons.

**Hardware debounce:** a capacitor from the pin to GND. The button discharges it instantly, but on release it can only recharge slowly through the pull-up: **τ = R·C**. The voltage needs t = −RC·ln(1 − 0.6) ≈ **0.92·RC** to cross the 3.0 V HIGH threshold — the bounces are over long before that. The Schmitt trigger turns the slow ramp into one edge.

**Software debounce:** ignore further edges for a "lockout" time after the first one (the reaction timer does this), or only accept a new state after it has been stable for N ms.

### Interrupts done right
`attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), isr, FALLING)` runs `isr()` the instant pin 2 falls — in the middle of whatever loop() was doing. On the Uno only **pins 2 and 3** have these external interrupts (others have "pin-change" interrupts, which need more code).

Rules:
1. **Keep ISRs tiny:** grab a timestamp, set a flag, increment a counter. No Serial, no delay().
2. Variables shared with loop() must be **`volatile`**, or the compiler may keep a stale copy in a register.
3. Multi-byte variables (int, long) are read in several steps on an 8-bit CPU. An interrupt can strike in between and you read half-old, half-new bytes. Copy them inside **`noInterrupts()` … `interrupts()`**.
4. `micros()` has a resolution of **4 µs** on a 16 MHz Uno — plenty for a human, but know it.

Why time a reaction in an interrupt? Because if loop() is busy printing for 3 ms when you press, polling would add up to 3 ms of error. The ISR grabs `micros()` within a few microseconds of the edge.

- **Floating input** — Undefined state; picks up noise. Fix with a pull-up/down.
- **INPUT_PULLUP value (ATmega328P)** — ≈ 20–50 kΩ to Vcc

units.title: Three Pins, Eight Outputs

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Shift registers, latches, decoupling and the 7-segment display

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Explain serial-in / parallel-out and why the 74HC595 has a separate latch
- Respect per-pin and per-chip current limits when driving LEDs
- Know why every logic chip gets a 100 nF decoupling capacitor
- Map segments to bits and build glyphs for a 7-segment display

content:
### Serial in, parallel out
The 74HC595 contains **two** 8-bit registers:
1. A **shift register**. Every rising edge on **SHCP** (shift clock, pin 11) moves all bits one place along and takes in a new bit from **DS** (data, pin 14).
2. A **storage register (latch)**. A rising edge on **STCP** (pin 12) copies the shift register into it in one go. The outputs Q0–Q7 show the *latch*, not the shift register.

That separation is the clever part: while you clock 8 new bits in, the outputs don't flicker through the intermediate patterns. You raise the latch once and all 8 outputs change at the same instant.

Other pins: **/OE** (13) enables the outputs when LOW — PWM it and you dim all 8 LEDs at once. **/MR** (10) clears the shift register when LOW — tie it to 5 V. **Q7'** (9) is the bit that falls off the end: wire it to the next 595's DS and you can chain as many chips as you like, still using only three Arduino pins.

`shiftOut(data, clock, MSBFIRST, value)` *bit-bangs* this protocol in software. The same chip can also be driven by the Uno's hardware **SPI** (MOSI = D11 → DS, SCK = D13 → SHCP) far faster — a preview of Unit 11.

### Current limits — the chip's, not just the LED's
74HC595 (TI datasheet): ±35 mA per output, but only **±70 mA total through VCC or GND**. Eight LEDs at 10 mA = 80 mA → over the limit. With **1 kΩ** per LED you get ~3 mA each (24 mA total), still clearly visible with modern LEDs. Always add up the totals.

### Decoupling: the 100 nF next to every chip
When eight outputs switch at once, the chip suddenly needs current. The breadboard wires back to the Arduino have inductance, so the supply at the chip's pin sags for a moment (V = L·dI/dt again!) — the chip can glitch or reset. A **100 nF ceramic capacitor right across VCC–GND** acts as a tiny local tank that supplies those spikes. Every digital IC on every professional board has one. It costs nothing; leaving it out costs evenings.

### 7-segment displays
Seven LED bars a–g plus a decimal point (dp). In a **common-cathode** display all cathodes are joined (to GND) and you drive each anode HIGH; common-anode is the reverse (common to +5 V, drive segments LOW). Map Q0→a, Q1→b … Q6→g, Q7→dp, and each digit is one byte: "0" lights a, b, c, d, e, f = bits 0–5 = **0x3F**.

```
   a          bit: 7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0
  ---         seg: dp g  f  e  d  c  b  a
f|   |b
  -g-          "7" = a b c        = 0x07
e|   |c        "8" = all but dp   = 0x7F
  ---  .dp
   d
```

Several digits are **multiplexed**: light digit 1 for 2 ms, then digit 2, and so on. Above ~50–60 refreshes per second your eye blends them (persistence of vision), and you need 8 + N pins instead of 8 × N.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| LED current per output | I = (5 V − Vf) / R |
| 595 chip budget | Σ I(outputs) ≤ 70 mA through VCC/GND |
| Pins for N chained 595s | 3 pins → 8·N outputs |

**Remember**

- **SHCP / STCP on a 595** — Shift clock (moves bits in) / storage clock (latches to outputs)
- **/OE on a 595** — Active-LOW output enable — PWM it to dim all outputs
- **Q7'** — Serial out — feeds the next 595 in a chain
- **74HC595 current limits** — ±35 mA per output, ±70 mA total through VCC/GND
- **Decoupling capacitor** — 100 nF ceramic across every chip's VCC–GND, as close as possible
- **Common cathode vs common anode** — CC: commons to GND, drive segments HIGH. CA: commons to +V, drive LOW.
- **'0' on a,b,c,d,e,f = bits 0–5** — 0x3F
- **Multiplexing** — Light one digit at a time, fast; needs segments + digits pins instead of segments × digits

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: The ADC, resistive sensors, calibration, filtering and hysteresis

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Know the ADC's resolution, speed, references and quantisation error
- Use ratiometric dividers so the supply voltage cancels out
- Turn a thermistor's resistance into °C with the Beta equation, and calibrate Beta yourself
- Filter noisy readings and stop a threshold from chattering with hysteresis

content:
### The ATmega's ADC in numbers
- **10 bits** → 1024 levels. With the 5 V reference, 1 LSB = 5/1024 = **4.88 mV**.
- **Successive approximation:** it tries the MSB, compares, keeps or drops it, then the next bit — 10 comparisons, like a binary search.
- Default ADC clock 125 kHz, 13 clocks per conversion → ~104 µs, so **analogRead() takes about 0.11 ms** (~9 000 readings/s). Capstone 2 speeds this up.
- **Quantisation error:** ±½ LSB, because a continuous voltage gets rounded to a step.
- **References:** `DEFAULT` (AVcc, ~5 V), `INTERNAL` (1.1 V bandgap: 1.07 mV per step, great for small signals), `EXTERNAL` (whatever you put on AREF).

### Ratiometric measurement
Put a resistive sensor in a divider fed from the **same** 5 V that the ADC uses as reference. Then

ADC / 1024 = R_sensor / (R_fixed + R_sensor)

and **the supply voltage cancels out completely**. A sagging USB rail can't fool you. Solving for the sensor:

**R_sensor = R_fixed · ADC / (1024 − ADC)** (sensor on the bottom)

Choose R_fixed ≈ the sensor's resistance in the middle of the range you care about; that's where the divider is most sensitive.

### NTC thermistors and the Beta equation
An NTC's resistance falls as temperature rises — and not linearly. The **Beta model** is good to a fraction of a degree over a few tens of degrees:

**1/T = 1/T₀ + (1/B) · ln(R/R₀)**, temperatures in **kelvin** (T₀ = 298.15 K = 25 °C, R₀ = 10 kΩ for your part)

B is usually 3435 or 3950 for 10 kΩ parts, but kits rarely tell you which. So you'll **measure** it: record R at two known temperatures T₁, T₂ and

**B = ln(R₁/R₂) / (1/T₁ − 1/T₂)**

(The Steinhart-Hart equation adds terms for higher accuracy over wide ranges.)

### Light-dependent resistors
CdS cells go from ~1 MΩ in the dark to ~1 kΩ in bright light, roughly logarithmically, and they're **slow** — tens of ms to react, longer to recover from bright light. Perfect for night lights; a real limitation for the optical data link in Unit 11.

### Filtering noise
- **Averaging N readings** reduces random noise by **√N** (16 readings → 4× less noise).
- **Exponential moving average:** `smooth += α · (raw − smooth)`, with α between 0 and 1. Small α = smoother but slower. It's the digital twin of the RC low-pass from Unit 3: one memory, no array.

### Hysteresis
A single threshold plus a noisy signal sitting right at it = output chattering on and off. Use **two thresholds**: switch ON below the low one, OFF above the high one. Between them, keep the previous state. Your thermostat at home does exactly this.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| ADC step size | LSB = Vref / 1024 |
| Sensor from divider (sensor at bottom) | R = R_fixed · ADC / (1024 − ADC) |
| Beta equation | 1/T = 1/T₀ + ln(R/R₀)/B   (kelvin) |
| Beta from two points | B = ln(R₁/R₂) / (1/T₁ − 1/T₂) |
| Averaging | noise ÷ √N |
| Exponential moving average | y ← y + α(x − y) |

**Remember**

- **Uno ADC** — 10 bit, 0–1023, ~0.11 ms per analogRead()
- **1 LSB at 5 V / 1.1 V reference** — 4.88 mV / 1.07 mV
- **Ratiometric** — Sensor divider and ADC reference from the same supply → supply cancels
- **Sensor on bottom of divider** — R = R_fixed · ADC / (1024 − ADC)
- **Beta equation** — 1/T = 1/T₀ + ln(R/R₀)/B, T in kelvin
- **NTC** — Negative temperature coefficient: hotter → lower resistance
- **Averaging N samples** — Noise drops by √N
- **EMA filter** — y += α(x − y); small α = smooth & slow
- **Hysteresis** — Separate ON and OFF thresholds; hold state in between

units.title: Echoes & Tones
units.description: Frequency, wavelength and the speed of sound — a sonar theremin

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Frequency, wavelength and the speed of sound — a sonar theremin

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Move fluently between frequency, period and wavelength
- Measure distance by time of flight and correct for air temperature
- Generate square-wave tones and understand what tone() borrows from the chip
- Map a sensor to a musical scale (equal temperament, pentatonic)

content:
### Frequency, period, wavelength
**f = 1 / T**. A wave travelling at speed v has wavelength **λ = v / f**. In air at 20 °C, sound travels at about **343 m/s**:
- a 1 kHz tone has λ ≈ 34 cm,
- the HC-SR04's 40 kHz ultrasound has λ ≈ 8.6 mm.

The speed of sound depends on temperature: **c ≈ 331.3 + 0.606·T** m/s (T in °C). From 20 °C to 30 °C it changes by ~1.8 % — and so does your distance reading, unless you correct for it (Unit 7's thermistor can).

### Time-of-flight ranging
The HC-SR04 sends a short burst of 40 kHz pulses when you give TRIG a 10 µs HIGH pulse. It then raises ECHO and keeps it HIGH until the reflection comes back. The pulse width is the **round-trip** time, so:

**distance = c · t / 2**

With c = 343 m/s = 0.0343 cm/µs: distance (cm) ≈ t (µs) / 58.3. One microsecond of timing = 0.17 mm. The real limits are acoustic: a ~15° beam, soft or angled surfaces that don't echo back, ~2 cm minimum range, and leftover echoes — wait ~60 ms between pings.

`pulseIn(pin, HIGH, timeout)` measures a pulse width in µs. It **blocks** until the pulse ends or the timeout passes — always give it a timeout (30 ms ≈ 5 m round trip).

### Making sound
- An **active** buzzer has its own oscillator: give it DC and it beeps at one fixed pitch.
- A **passive** buzzer is just a piezo disc: *you* supply the waveform, so you choose the pitch.

`tone(pin, freq)` generates a 50 % square wave using **Timer2**. Side effect: PWM on pins **3 and 11** (also Timer2) stops working while a tone plays. Timers are shared hardware. Knowing which library uses which timer saves hours (Servo uses Timer1 → no PWM on 9 and 10).

A square wave isn't a pure tone: it contains odd harmonics (3f, 5f, 7f…) — that's why it sounds buzzy.

### Music in numbers
Equal temperament: each semitone multiplies frequency by **2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595**, an octave by 2. A4 = 440 Hz, A5 = 880 Hz, C5 ≈ 523 Hz. A **pentatonic** scale (C D E G A) has no "clashing" neighbours, so a theremin quantised to it always sounds musical — that's the trick in this lab.

content.alt: HC-SR04 on D7/D6, passive buzzer on D8 with a series resistor to tame the volume.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Frequency ↔ period | f = 1/T |
| Wavelength | λ = v / f |
| Speed of sound | c ≈ 331.3 + 0.606·T(°C)  m/s |
| Sonar distance | d = c · t / 2   (≈ t[µs] / 58 cm) |
| Semitone | f(n) = 440 · 2^(n/12) |

**Remember**

- **Speed of sound vs temperature** — c ≈ 331.3 + 0.606·T(°C) m/s (343 m/s at 20 °C)
- **Sonar distance** — d = c·t/2 ≈ t[µs]/58 cm
- **Wavelength** — λ = v/f
- **tone() side effect** — Uses Timer2 → no PWM on pins 3 and 11
- **Servo library side effect** — Uses Timer1 → no PWM on pins 9 and 10
- **Semitone ratio** — 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595; octave = ×2
- **Active vs passive buzzer** — Active: own oscillator, DC on/off. Passive: you drive the waveform.
- **pulseIn() danger** — Blocks until the pulse ends — always pass a timeout

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Build an oscillator with no code — then measure it two different ways

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Explain how a 555 astable oscillates using two comparators and a flip-flop
- Calculate frequency and duty cycle from R1, R2 and C — and measure the real thing
- See the timing capacitor bounce between 1/3 and 2/3 of Vcc
- Compare gate counting and period measurement and know when each wins

content:
### Inside the 555
Three equal resistors from Vcc to GND make two reference voltages: **⅓ Vcc** and **⅔ Vcc**. Two comparators watch the timing capacitor:
- When the cap rises above **⅔ Vcc** (THR, pin 6) → the internal flip-flop resets → output LOW, and the **discharge transistor** (DIS, pin 7) turns on.
- When the cap falls below **⅓ Vcc** (TRG, pin 2) → flip-flop sets → output HIGH, discharge transistor off.

### The astable circuit
- **Charging:** through R1 + R2 from ⅓ to ⅔ Vcc. The output is HIGH.
- **Discharging:** through R2 only, into pin 7, from ⅔ back to ⅓ Vcc. The output is LOW.

Going from ⅓ to ⅔ of the way (or back) on an RC curve always takes τ·ln 2 = **0.693·τ** — whatever Vcc is. So:

- **t_high = 0.693 · (R1 + R2) · C**
- **t_low = 0.693 · R2 · C**
- **f = 1 / (0.693 · (R1 + 2·R2) · C) ≈ 1.44 / ((R1 + 2R2)·C)**
- **duty = (R1 + R2) / (R1 + 2R2)** — always above 50 % in this basic circuit (a diode across R2 fixes that)

With R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ: C = 10 µF gives ~6.9 Hz (a visible blink); C = 100 nF gives ~687 Hz (an audible tone). Same circuit, one part swapped.

Pin 4 (RESET) goes to Vcc. Pin 5 (CTRL) exposes the ⅔ reference — a **10 nF** cap to GND keeps noise out of it. The classic NE555 is bipolar, pulls ~3–10 mA by itself and its output stage can source/sink ~200 mA. The CMOS 7555/TLC555 sips µA and swings closer to the rails.

### Measuring frequency: two methods
**Gate counting:** count rising edges for a fixed gate time (1 s). Result = count / gate. Resolution is **±1 count**, so ±1 Hz with a 1 s gate. At 687 Hz that's 0.15 % — excellent. At 6.9 Hz it's ±15 % — useless.

**Period (reciprocal) measurement:** time one cycle with a fast clock (pulseIn() measures in µs). Resolution is a few µs per period. At 6.9 Hz (145 ms period) that's 0.003 %; at 100 kHz (10 µs) it's terrible. It also gives you the **duty cycle**.

Real counters do both and pick the better one automatically — so will your Bench Meter in Capstone 1.

### Why the measured value won't match exactly
Electrolytics are ±20 %, ceramics ±10–20 % (cheap ones far worse), resistors ±5 %. A 555 built from kit parts lands within ~20 % of the formula. The formula is the design target, the meter tells you the truth.

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: H-bridges, servos, steppers — and your first closed control loop

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Drive a DC motor in both directions with an H-bridge, and know brake vs coast
- Explain the voltage lost in a bipolar driver like the L293D
- Generate servo pulses and understand what's inside a hobby servo
- Build and tune a proportional controller (the sun tracker) and see what too much gain does

content:
### The DC motor as a circuit
A spinning motor is also a generator. It produces a **back-EMF** proportional to its speed that opposes the supply: I = (V − E_back) / R_winding. At standstill E_back = 0, so the **stall current** is V / R — often 3–10× the running current. That's the spike that resets Arduinos sharing a supply with a motor.

### The H-bridge
Four switches arranged like the letter H with the motor as the crossbar. Close top-left + bottom-right → current flows one way. Close the other diagonal → it flows the other way. Two forbidden states: both switches on the **same side** on at once = a dead short across the supply (**shoot-through**). Driver chips prevent this for you.

L293D logic (EN high):

| 1A | 2A | Motor |
|---|---|---|
| H | L | forward |
| L | H | reverse |
| L | L | **brake** — both terminals tied together, back-EMF current stops it fast |
| H | H | **brake** (same idea, tied to +V) |
| EN LOW: any | any | **coast** — outputs float, it spins down freely |

The L293D uses bipolar (Darlington-style) output transistors. Each conducting switch drops more than a volt, and two are in the path, so the motor typically sees **~1.5–3 V less than the supply**, more at higher currents. That lost voltage × current becomes heat. MOSFET drivers (TB6612FNG, DRV8833) lose a fraction of that — a good reason they replaced it. The "D" in L293D means the flyback diodes from Unit 4 are built in.

### Servos are closed-loop systems in a box
A hobby servo contains a motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer on the output shaft and a small controller. You send a pulse every **20 ms (50 Hz)**; the pulse **width** is the target angle: ~1.0 ms at one end, **1.5 ms in the middle**, ~2.0 ms at the other (many SG90s accept ~0.5–2.4 ms for the full 180°). The controller compares the target with the pot and drives the motor to remove the difference. Moving servos draw current spikes of several hundred mA — give them a capacitor and ideally their own 5 V.

### Steppers are open-loop
A stepper moves a fixed angle per coil pattern step. The 28BYJ-48 has 32 steps per motor revolution and a ~64:1 gearbox → **~2048 steps per output revolution** in full-step mode. No sensor: the Arduino assumes every step happened. Push it too fast and it silently skips steps, and from then on its position is wrong. The ULN2003 board is a Darlington array with built-in flyback diodes.

### Closing the loop: proportional control
Every controller has the same parts: a **setpoint** (what you want), a **measurement**, the **error** = setpoint − measurement, and an **action**. The simplest useful one:

**action = K_P · error**

In the sun tracker, the error is the difference between the left and right LDR readings, and the action moves the servo. Small K_P: slow but stable. Bigger K_P: faster… until it **overshoots**, swings back, and **oscillates**. A **deadband** ignores tiny errors so it doesn't twitch at noise. Real systems add an Integral term (removes leftover steady error) and a Derivative term (damps overshoot): that's **PID**, the most used algorithm in all of engineering.

**Formula sheet**

|---|---|
| Motor current | I = (V − E_back) / R_winding;  stall: I = V / R |
| Driver loss | P_driver ≈ V_drop · I |

**Remember**

- **Back-EMF** — Voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply; ∝ speed
- **Stall current** — V / R_winding — the big inrush spike
- **H-bridge brake vs coast** — Brake: terminals shorted (fast stop). Coast: outputs floating.
- **Shoot-through** — Both switches on one side on → supply short
- **L293D drawback** — Bipolar outputs lose ~1.5–3 V total → heat
- **Servo signal** — 50 Hz, pulse ~1–2 ms sets angle (1.5 ms = middle)
- **28BYJ-48 steps per revolution** — ≈ 2048 (full-step)
- **P controller** — u = K_P · error; too much gain → oscillation
- **PID** — Proportional + Integral (kills steady error) + Derivative (damps overshoot)

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Draw a UART frame bit by bit and explain why the receiver samples mid-bit
- Compute data rates and clock-tolerance limits
- Compare UART, I²C and SPI: wires, addressing, speed, open-drain vs push-pull
- Drive an HD44780 LCD in 4-bit mode and create custom characters

content:
### UART: asynchronous serial
There is no shared clock wire. Both ends agree on a **baud rate** in advance, and every byte carries its own synchronisation:

- The line **idles HIGH**.
- **Start bit:** one bit time LOW. The falling edge tells the receiver "a byte starts now".
- **8 data bits, least significant bit first.**
- Optional parity bit.
- **Stop bit(s):** HIGH, at least one bit time. This guarantees the next start bit makes a fresh falling edge.

"**8N1**" = 8 data, no parity, 1 stop → **10 bits per byte**. So 9600 baud carries 960 bytes/s; 115 200 baud carries 11 520 bytes/s.

The receiver spots the start edge, waits **1.5 bit times** to land in the middle of data bit 0, then samples once per bit time. Sampling in the middle gives the most margin. Because the two clocks are independent, a small mismatch accumulates over the frame. By the stop bit (9.5 bit times in) the error must stay under half a bit: roughly **±5 % total mismatch**, in practice ±2 % per side.

The Uno's USB-serial chip (an ATmega16U2) converts this 0/5 V "TTL serial" to USB. Old RS-232 ports use ±3 to ±15 V with inverted logic — never connect those to an Arduino pin directly.

### Your light link is a real UART
The LED is the transmitter: light = 1 (idle), dark = 0. The LDR is the receiver. The code in this lab implements the frame by hand, with **two stop bits** to give the slow LDR time to recover. When you raise the baud rate, the LDR's response time (Unit 7: tens of ms) eventually blurs neighbouring bits together. You'll find the *bandwidth* of your channel by breaking it.

### I²C: two wires, many chips
**SDA** (data) and **SCL** (clock), shared by every device on the bus. Lines are **open-drain**: devices can only pull them LOW; **pull-up resistors** (typically 4.7 kΩ) pull them HIGH. That's why two chips can never fight (one HIGH, one LOW = short circuit) — a pull-down always wins safely. Each device has a **7-bit address**, and every byte is answered with an ACK bit. Standard 100 kHz, fast 400 kHz. On the Uno: **A4 = SDA, A5 = SCL**.

### SPI: fast and simple
**SCK** (clock), **MOSI** (master out), **MISO** (master in) and one **CS** (chip select, active LOW) per device. Full-duplex (data both ways at once), push-pull, no addresses, no ACK, up to 8 MHz on the Uno. On the Uno: D13 SCK, D11 MOSI, D12 MISO, D10 default SS. The 74HC595 from Unit 6 is basically an SPI output device.

### The HD44780 LCD (a parallel interface)
The 1602 LCD's controller takes 8-bit data, but in **4-bit mode** you send each byte as two nibbles on D4–D7. **RS** selects command (0) or character (1), **E** is the strobe: data is read on its falling edge. **RW** tied to GND = we only write. **V0** sets contrast (a pot) — if you see nothing or black boxes, it's almost always V0. The controller has **8 slots of CGRAM** for your own 5×8-pixel characters.

units.title: Where Does the Power Go?
units.description: Regulators, batteries, current budgets and sleep modes

lessons.title: Theory
lessons.summary: Regulators, batteries, current budgets and sleep modes

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Calculate linear-regulator heat and efficiency, and know when a switching regulator wins
- Measure real current consumption with the meter in series
- Estimate battery life, including duty-cycled designs
- Use AVR sleep modes and understand why an Uno board can't really sleep

content:
### Linear regulators burn the difference
A linear regulator (like the Uno's NCP1117 on the barrel jack / VIN path) works like a smart variable resistor: the input current equals the output current. Everything between Vin and Vout becomes heat:

**P_loss = (Vin − Vout) · I**, efficiency **η = Vout / Vin**

Feed 9 V into an Uno drawing 50 mA: 0.2 W of heat and only 56 % efficiency. Feed it 12 V at 200 mA: 1.4 W — the regulator gets too hot to touch and shuts down. That's why the recommended input is 7–12 V, and why "more voltage is safer" is false.

### Switching regulators
A **buck** converter chops the input with a fast switch and smooths it with an inductor and capacitor (the PWM + filter idea from Unit 3, with an inductor). Efficiency 80–95 % and nearly independent of Vin. A **boost** converter goes the other way (e.g. 3.7 V Li-ion → 5 V). Because power in ≈ power out / η, a buck *reduces* the current drawn from the battery when Vin > Vout — a linear regulator never can.

### Batteries
Capacity is in **mAh**: 500 mAh ≈ 500 mA for 1 h, or 5 mA for 100 h — roughly. High currents deliver less (internal resistance, chemistry), so treat datasheet capacity as a best case. A 9 V alkaline is ~500 mAh at low drain, an AA alkaline ~2000–2500 mAh.

**Battery life ≈ capacity / average current.**

Most battery gadgets sleep 99 % of the time. Their *average* current is:

**I_avg = (I_active · t_active + I_sleep · t_sleep) / (t_active + t_sleep)**

Which means the sleep current often matters more than the active current!

### Sleep modes on the ATmega328P
- `delay()` does **not** save power — the CPU spins in a loop counting.
- **IDLE:** CPU clock stops, peripherals and timers keep running. Any interrupt (including the 1 ms millis() tick) wakes it.
- **POWER-DOWN:** almost everything off, including the main oscillator. Only external interrupts (on INT0/INT1, as a **LOW level** — edge detection needs a clock that is stopped), pin changes, the watchdog or I²C address match can wake it. A bare ATmega328P in power-down with the watchdog and brown-out detector off draws **well under 1 µA**.

### …but the Uno board isn't a bare chip
The Uno also powers a USB-serial chip (16U2), a power LED, regulators and an op-amp. Those draw tens of mA whatever the main chip does. You're about to measure how little sleep helps on an Uno — and that's the lesson: low-power products are designed from the board up (bare chip, efficient regulator, no LEDs, sensors switched off).

### Measuring current
Meter on **mA**, red lead in the **mA socket**, meter **in series** with the supply. The meter's shunt adds a small *burden voltage* (≈ mV per mA on low ranges), and fast current spikes are averaged out — a meter shows the average.

content.caption: Battery into VIN with the meter in series on the + lead. USB unplugged!

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Linear regulator loss | P = (Vin − Vout) · I |
| Linear efficiency | η = Vout / Vin |
| Switching regulator input current | I_in = Vout · I_out / (η · Vin) |
| Battery life | t ≈ capacity / I_avg |
| Duty-cycled average | I_avg = (I_a·t_a + I_s·t_s)/(t_a + t_s) |

**Remember**

- **Linear regulator heat** — (Vin − Vout) × I
- **Linear regulator efficiency** — Vout / Vin
- **Buck converter** — Switching step-down, 80–95 % efficient; draws LESS input current than output when Vin > Vout
- **Battery life** — capacity [mAh] / average current [mA] = hours
- **delay() and power** — Busy-wait — saves nothing
- **ATmega328P power-down** — < 1 µA bare chip (WDT and BOD off); wake by INT0/1 LOW level, pin change, WDT
- **Why the Uno can't sleep well** — USB chip, power LED, regulators, op-amp keep drawing tens of mA
- **Uno recommended VIN** — 7–12 V

1. Upload u12_sleep_current over USB FIRST, then unplug USB. VIN bypasses the Uno's reverse-polarity protection: double-check + and − before connecting.
2. Connect the battery through the meter. The on-board LED blinks once: mode 0 (busy).

4. Press the button: mode 1 (busy + LED on).
5. **Write down:** Mode 1 — BUSY + LED current. (mA)
6. Press: mode 2 (IDLE sleep).

8. Press: mode 3 (POWER-DOWN). Press again to wake it.

units.description: Your own 4-mode instrument — volts, ohms, capacitance, frequency — on an LCD

lessons.title: The plan
lessons.summary: Your own 4-mode instrument — volts, ohms, capacitance, frequency — on an LCD

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Plan a pin budget when several circuits share one microcontroller
- Combine four measurement front-ends with one mode button and an LCD
- Calibrate an instrument and analyse its accuracy across its range

content:
Every mode of this instrument is a circuit you've already built — the skill now is **system design**: fitting them together without conflicts, calibrating them, and knowing where your meter is accurate and where it isn't.

### Pin budget

| Function | Pins | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency input | **D2** | needs an external interrupt (INT0) |
| Mode button | **D3** | the only other interrupt-capable pin (polled here, free for later) |
| LCD RS, E, D4–D7 | D12, D11, D4–D7 | moved off D2/D3 compared with Unit 11! |
| Capacitance charge / discharge | D8 / D9 | |
| Continuity buzzer | D10 | tone() uses Timer2 → don't need PWM on 3/11 anyway |
| Volts / Cap / Ohms sense | A0 / A1 / A2 | |

### The four modes
- **VOLTS:** a 30 k / 10 k divider (ratio 4) lets A0 see up to 20 V. The bandgap trick from Unit 1 corrects for your real 5 V rail. DC only, positive only.
- **OHMS:** 5 V → 10 kΩ reference → A2 → Rx → GND. Ratiometric (Unit 7): **Rx = R_ref · ADC / (1024 − ADC)**, no Vcc dependence. Below 50 Ω it beeps as a continuity tester.
- **CAP:** the RC timing meter from Unit 3.
- **FREQ:** gate counting for ≥ 100 Hz, period timing below — the automatic choice from Unit 9.

### Where is the ohmmeter accurate?
A divider's output changes fastest when Rx ≈ R_ref. Near the ends, one ADC count covers a big range of resistance: with R_ref = 10 kΩ, 100 Ω gives ADC ≈ 10 (each count ≈ 10 %!) and 1 MΩ gives ADC ≈ 1014 (one count from "OPEN"). Real meters switch reference resistors — *autoranging* — which is the first challenge.

> ⚠ The volts input is for low-voltage DC only (≤ 20 V, never negative). It is not a mains multimeter and never will be.

**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| Volts mode | V = ADC · Vcc / 1024 · (R_top + R_bottom)/R_bottom |
| Ohms mode | Rx = R_ref · ADC / (1024 − ADC) |
| Cap mode | C = τ / R_charge |
| Freq mode | f = edges / 1 s   or   f = 1 / (t_high + t_low) |

**Remember**

- **Ohmmeter from a divider** — Rx = R_ref · ADC / (1024 − ADC); best accuracy near R_ref
- **Autoranging** — Switch reference resistors so the reading lands mid-scale
- **Pin budgeting** — Allocate the scarce pins (interrupts, PWM/timers, ADC) first

### Step by step

1. Build and test the LCD alone first (upload the Unit 11 dashboard with the pin numbers changed to 12, 11, 4, 5, 6, 7).
2. Build the front-ends one at a time. Measure every resistor with your multimeter and write the real values down.
3. **Predict** → lab test, question 1: Your divider is 3 × 10 kΩ on top and 10 kΩ at the bottom. What is DIVIDER_RATIO?
4. Enter DIVIDER_RATIO, R_REF, R_CHARGE (measured) and BANDGAP_mV (from Unit 1) at the top of c1_bench_meter. Upload.
5. **Measure** → lab test, question 2: VOLTS mode: probe the Arduino's own 3.3V pin.

7. **Measure** → lab test, question 3: OHMS mode: 10 kΩ resistor.

9. **Measure** → lab test, question 5: OHMS mode: 100 kΩ resistor.

lessons.title: The plan
lessons.summary: Sampling, triggering, Nyquist and aliasing — see your circuits move

content.text:
**In this unit you will**

- Trade ADC precision for speed by changing the prescaler
- Implement a rising-edge trigger and a timebase
- Measure frequency, duty cycle and Vpp from a buffer of samples
- Demonstrate aliasing and explain the Nyquist limit

content:
An oscilloscope is a fast ADC, a memory buffer, a trigger and a display. You have all four.

### Going faster
The ADC clock is the 16 MHz system clock divided by a **prescaler** (default 128 → 125 kHz). One conversion takes 13 ADC clocks. Set the prescaler to 16 → 1 MHz ADC clock → 13 µs per conversion, roughly **50–60 k samples/s** with analogRead()'s overhead. The datasheet only guarantees full 10-bit accuracy up to 200 kHz ADC clock — at 1 MHz you lose a couple of effective bits. Speed vs. precision: a real engineering trade.

### Trigger
Without a trigger every capture starts at a random point and a repeating signal looks like it's sliding around. The sketch waits for the signal to be **below** the trigger level and then **cross above** it (a rising edge), and only then fills the buffer. Every capture now starts at the same point of the waveform → a stable picture. AUTO mode gives up after 100 ms and captures anyway (so you see flat lines too); NORMAL mode only draws when triggered.

### Sampling theory in one paragraph
You only know the signal at the sample instants. **Nyquist:** to represent a frequency f you must sample faster than **2f**. Sample slower and higher frequencies don't disappear — they **masquerade as lower ones (aliasing)**: a signal at f sampled at f_s shows up at |f − k·f_s| for the nearest whole k. A square wave also contains harmonics at 3f, 5f, 7f…, so to see its *shape* you want f_s ≥ 10× f.

> ⚠ The probe input is 0–5 V only. The 1 kΩ series resistor limits current if you slip, but it is not protection against higher voltages.

content.text:
**Formula sheet**

|  | Formula |
|---|---|
| ADC clock | f_ADC = 16 MHz / prescaler; conversion = 13 ADC clocks |
| Nyquist | f_s > 2 · f_max |
| Alias frequency | f_alias = \|f − k·f_s\|, k = round(f / f_s) |
| Capture window | T = N · Δt |

**Remember**

- **Nyquist criterion** — Sample faster than 2 × the highest frequency present
- **Aliasing** — Undersampled f appears at |f − k·fs|
- **Trigger** — Start each capture at the same level crossing → stable picture
- **ADC prescaler trade-off** — Faster ADC clock → more samples/s but fewer effective bits (>200 kHz)

### Step by step

1. Link D5 → 1 kΩ → A0. Upload c2_scope. Open Serial Monitor to see the '#' measurement lines, then the Serial Plotter to see the trace.
2. **Write down:** Sample rate (fs) reported with the fastest timebase. (kS/s)
3. **Measure** → lab test, question 1: Frequency the scope reports for the 1 000 Hz test tone.
4. **Predict** → lab test, question 2: At about 16 µs per sample, how long is a 400-sample capture window?
5. Probe your fast 555 output (100 nF version) instead of the test tone.
6. **Measure** → lab test, question 3: Duty cycle the scope reports for the 555.
7. Probe the 555's timing capacitor (pin 6). Press '+' until the window shows a few cycles: the shark-fin from Unit 9, now at 687 Hz.
8. Probe your PWM-RC filter (1 kΩ + 10 µF) output: see the ripple riding on the DC level. Read Vmin/Vmax.
9. **Write down:** Ripple Vpp (Vmax − Vmin) on the RC filter. (V)
10. Aliasing: re-link D5 → A0. Press '+' until the timebase is the slowest (fs ≈ 0.5 kS/s). Send 't' until the test tone is 1 000 Hz, then 3 000 Hz.
11. **Write down:** Frequency the scope reports for the 3 000 Hz tone at the slowest timebase. (Hz)
12. **Check** → lab test, question 4: The scope shows a slow wave even though the tone is 3 kHz. What happened?

At full speed you can see a 1 kHz square wave's edges and a 555's ramps. At the slowest timebase a fast signal turns into a convincing — but completely fake — slow one.

### If it doesn't work

- **Flat line at 0 or 5 V** — Probe not connected, or no common ground with the circuit under test.
- **Picture slides around** — Trigger level (512 = 2.5 V) is outside the signal's range — the scope fell back to AUTO.
- **Plotter is unreadable with '#' lines** — Read the measurements in Serial Monitor, the trace in the Plotter, or send 'c' and paste the CSV into a spreadsheet.
